introduction-the-power-failure-nightmare.core: A single logical operation, such as appending to a file, touches several disk locations: data blocks, the inode (size, timestamps), free-space bitmaps and the directory entry. If power fails midway, some writes land and others don't, leaving the filesystem inconsistent (leaked blocks, corrupted metadata, files pointing to garbage). Filesystem integrity techniques (journaling, copy-on-write, barriers, checksums) exist to survive that.

first_principles.problem: After a power cut, a server spends an hour in fsck and some files contain blocks from other files.

analogy.title: Moving house mid-way through a blackout
analogy.story: Half your boxes are in the new house and the address register still says the old one; nobody knows where anything is.
analogy.breaks: Moves can be redone by hand; filesystems need automatic recovery.

example.title: One append
flow: Crash after step 3 before step 2 → inode points to stale data

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows why ordering and atomicity matter.

check.q: Why can a power failure corrupt a filesystem even if each individual disk write is atomic?
check.a: A logical operation needs several writes; failing between them leaves metadata and data inconsistent.

journaling-the-write-ahead-log.core: Journaling filesystems (ext4, XFS) first write the intended changes to a journal, a write-ahead log, then commit a record, then apply the changes to their final locations, then mark the journal entry done. After a crash, the filesystem replays committed journal entries and discards incomplete ones, so recovery takes seconds instead of a full fsck. Modes trade safety for speed: data=journal (all data), data=ordered (the ext4 default: data before metadata commit), and data=writeback (metadata only).

first_principles.problem: Hour-long fsck runs after every unclean shutdown make recovery painfully slow.
truths: Logging intent first makes recovery possible.

analogy.title: A shopkeeper's ledger before stocking shelves
analogy.story: Write down 'moving 20 cans to aisle 3' first; if interrupted, the ledger says exactly what to finish or undo.
analogy.breaks: Ledgers are cheap; journaling data doubles write I/O.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Seconds of replay, not hours of fsck.

code.text:
mount | grep ' / '          # ext4 (rw,relatime,data=ordered)
dumpe2fs -h /dev/nvme0n1p1 2>/dev/null | grep -i journal
# after crash: kernel log shows 'EXT4-fs: recovery complete' in seconds

check.q: What does ext4's default data=ordered mode guarantee?
check.a: File data is written to disk before the related metadata is committed to the journal, preventing metadata pointing to stale data.

overwrite-vs-copy-on-write.core: Overwrite-in-place filesystems (ext4, XFS) update blocks where they live, relying on the journal for consistency. Copy-on-write filesystems (Btrfs, ZFS) never overwrite live data. They write new versions to free space, then atomically switch a root pointer up the tree, so the on-disk state is always consistent and snapshots are nearly free. The trade-offs are fragmentation for random-write workloads (databases, VM images) and write amplification.

first_principles.problem: A database on Btrfs slows over time due to fragmentation from constant random rewrites.
truths: Writing elsewhere then switching pointers is atomic.
derivation: Use **nodatacow** or overwrite FS for DBs.

analogy.title: Editing a document vs saving a new version
analogy.story: Overwriting changes pages in the binder; COW writes new pages and swaps the table of contents in one step.
analogy.breaks: Document versions are tidy; COW blocks scatter across disk.

example.title: COW update
flow: Write new parent pointing to B'
Atomically update superblock to new root

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Crash at any point leaves old or new tree intact.

check.q: Why are snapshots cheap on copy-on-write filesystems?
check.a: Old blocks are never overwritten, so a snapshot just keeps a reference to the old root; only changed blocks consume new space.

write-barriers-preventing-disk-lies.core: Disks and controllers cache writes and may reorder them, acknowledging data that's only in volatile cache. Journaling relies on ordering (journal before commit before checkpoint), so filesystems issue cache flushes and FUA (Force Unit Access) writes, known as barriers, to guarantee order and durability. Disabling barriers (nobarrier) for speed, or using drives that ignore flushes without power-loss protection, risks corruption on power loss. fsync() is the application's version.

first_principles.problem: A team mounts with nobarrier for performance, and a power cut corrupts the journal itself.

analogy.title: A courier who says 'delivered' while the parcel is still in the van
analogy.story: Unless you insist on a signed receipt (flush), 'delivered' might mean 'in the van'.
analogy.breaks: Couriers can be fired; consumer SSDs keep lying.

code.text:
fio --name=fsync --filename=/data/test --rw=write --bs=4k --size=256m --fsync=1 --ioengine=sync
# PLP enterprise SSD: ~30 µs fsync; consumer SSD: ~1–5 ms
mount | grep -c nobarrier   # should be 0

check.q: Why is mounting with nobarrier dangerous?
check.a: Without flushes and ordering guarantees, cached writes can reach disk out of order or be lost on power failure, breaking journal consistency.

bit-rot-and-checksums.core: Data can silently corrupt over time: media decay, firmware bugs, misdirected or lost writes, cable and controller errors. Drives' own ECC catches many errors but not all, and traditional filesystems (ext4, XFS) checksum only metadata, not data. ZFS and Btrfs checksum every block and verify on read; with redundancy (mirror, RAID-Z) they self-heal by reading a good copy, and periodic scrubs find latent corruption before you need the data.

first_principles.problem: A backup restore reveals photos with corrupted blocks that had been silently damaged for a year.

analogy.title: Sealed envelopes with a fingerprint
analogy.story: Each document has a fingerprint stored separately; any change is detected, and a duplicate copy replaces the damaged one.
analogy.breaks: Fingerprints are permanent; checksums must be stored apart from data to be trustworthy.

code.text:
zpool scrub tank
zpool status tank
#   scan: scrub repaired 128K in 02:14:31 with 0 errors
#   NAME        STATE  READ WRITE CKSUM
#   mirror-0    ONLINE    0     0     0
#     sdb       ONLINE    0     0     4   ← corrupted blocks healed from sdc

check.q: Why does RAID alone not protect against bit rot?
check.a: Traditional RAID can't tell which copy is correct without checksums; it may return or propagate corrupted data.

snapshots-the-time-machine.core: A snapshot is a point-in-time, read-only (or writable clone) view of a filesystem or volume. On COW filesystems (ZFS, Btrfs) and with LVM thin provisioning it's created instantly and initially uses no space, then grows as live data diverges. Snapshots enable quick rollback (bad upgrade), consistent backups (snapshot then copy), and replication (zfs send of incremental diffs). They aren't backups on their own, since they live on the same disks.

first_principles.problem: A package upgrade breaks a server, and restoring from backup would take hours.

analogy.title: Bookmarking a page in a changing book
analogy.story: You can flip back to exactly how it looked, but if the book burns, the bookmark goes with it.
analogy.breaks: Bookmarks cost nothing; snapshots consume space as data changes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Rollback in seconds; offsite copy incremental.

code.text:
zfs snapshot rpool/ROOT@pre-upgrade-2026-10-19
apt full-upgrade -y        # breaks things
zfs rollback rpool/ROOT@pre-upgrade-2026-10-19
# off-host incremental
zfs send -i @daily-1 tank/data@daily-2 | ssh backup zfs recv -F pool/data

check.q: Why is a snapshot not a substitute for a backup?
check.a: It lives on the same storage, so disk failure, pool corruption or ransomware with access can destroy it along with the data.
